Triggers.value: Feeling physically restrained or held down

Memory.value: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.

vignette:
At 76, Vannak had spent years building a life that looked steady from the outside. He lived alone, kept a strict routine, and still worked shifts in a warehouse, where he preferred predictable tasks and the physical certainty of moving boxes from one marked place to another. The event he returned to in treatment came from much earlier, when he was a civilian in a war zone in Southeast Asia. He described being taken during a sweep through his village, shoved to the ground, and pinned there while soldiers searched the area. What stayed with him was not only the fear that he might be killed, but the exact sensory pieces of it: the pressure of bodies and hands forcing him down, the smell of sweat, mud, and fuel, and the shouting that broke out around him as people argued, cried, and were ordered about. Even now, he could recount small details with unsettling precision, as if the scene had never really moved into the past.

In the years since, Vannak had not thought of himself as a man troubled by memories so much as a man who could be seized by them. He said that something in his surroundings could bring the whole scene back instantly, without warning, before he had time to prepare himself. If a coworker brushed too close behind him while they were unloading a truck and he felt hemmed in between pallets, the memory arrived in full detail: the ground under his face, the weight on his shoulders, the certainty that he could not move. In the warehouse, arguments between workers or the sharp tone of a supervisor confronting someone could have the same effect. Certain smells were especially potent. Diesel, stale sweat in summer heat, or damp cardboard mixed with chemical odors could pull the past directly into the present. When that happened, the memory was not vague or fragmentary. It was very clear and detailed, and he became so overwhelmed that he had to stop what he was doing, step away, and wait for the wave of feeling to settle.

Over time, the memories themselves had made his world feel increasingly full of danger. Because they returned so forcefully and with so much detail, Vannak had come to experience ordinary sensations as if they were loaded in advance. He noticed smells before other people did and tracked where they were coming from. In crowded aisles at work, he was quick to tense if someone stood too near him or if a forklift blocked his path and left him feeling boxed in. He was especially alert to raised voices. What frightened him most was how little warning he seemed to get. Since the memory could overtake him in an instant and leave him flooded with emotion, he moved through the day scanning for the kinds of touch, conflict, and smells that might set it off again. In this way the memory had taught him what to watch for, and the list of things that felt risky had gradually expanded within the narrow world of his shift.

That pattern had shaped his working life. He angled for tasks at the edges of the floor rather than in the busiest loading areas, and if tension started between coworkers he found a reason to leave before voices rose. He disliked situations where another worker had to squeeze past him in tight spaces between stacked goods. On bad days, even the ordinary jostling of warehouse work made his body go rigid. Once triggered, he could no longer keep the past at a distance; the memory came back with such force that he had to stop handling inventory and stand outside by the loading bay until he could breathe evenly again. The more often this happened, the more vividly he seemed to anticipate it, so that entering certain corners of the warehouse already felt dangerous because of the smells or the cramped layout.

Vannak sought help only after a recent confrontation at work. Two men began arguing near him while a truck idled at the dock, filling the area with exhaust. Someone trying to get around the dispute caught him by the arm to pull him back from a moving pallet jack. The combination of being grabbed, the shouting, and the smell brought the old scene back all at once. He dropped what he was carrying and was so overcome that he had to sit on the concrete outside, shaking and unable to go back in for some time. He was embarrassed by how exposed he felt, especially at his age, but what pushed him into treatment was not embarrassment alone. He was afraid that his world had become organized around the next sudden return of that memory, and he wanted, if possible, to stop living as though the past could seize him at any moment.
